meta.blurb: In the Thursday team meeting, Priya's hand goes halfway up and stays there. Then she lists small scary things, from saying hello to a neighbour to showing her secret drawings, and meets them one at a time, ten minutes each.
meta.bible: Priya: a young office worker who is shy at meetings and secretly loves drawing; kind, thoughtful and determined. Sam: Priya's friend who listens and admits that he also feels afraid. Mrs Okafor: Priya's elderly neighbour in her building. Dan: Priya's colleague whom she apologises to. Mr Grumble: Priya's name for her harsh inner voice. The year starts with a silent Thursday team meeting. Priya's brave list rates small scary acts from one to ten: greeting her neighbour is a two, a question in a meeting a five, sharing a drawing a nine, presenting to the team a seven. The ten-minute idea: one small brave act that takes ten minutes or less, with a timer. Ideas taught, in order: everyone feels fear; the body's alarm; avoidance makes fear grow; courage is acting while afraid; small steps; the brave list; compare what you feared with what happened; the spotlight effect; mistakes; kindness to yourself; the inner critic; asking for help; saying I don't know; saying no; apologising; sharing your work; sorting criticism; failing; rest; breaking a big act into ten-minute pieces. Facts are general and hedged: no invented studies or numbers. If fear stops someone living normally, a doctor or therapist can help; the book is general information and not a treatment. Voice and tone: warm, honest, encouraging and practical.

Priya wrote her question on a small piece of paper.
Priya said her question out loud in an empty room.

B1B2: In the team meeting, Priya has a good idea, but her hand will not go up. When the meeting ends, she walks back to her desk and feels annoyed with herself.
Priya thinks that other people never feel nervous, but she is wrong. Fear is a normal human feeling, and it does not mean that something is wrong with you.
When we are afraid, the body reacts at once. The heart beats faster, the hands become damp, and the breath gets short, because the body is getting ready to deal with danger.
The alarm system was built for physical danger, but it also goes off when we have to speak in front of others. In those cases it is often much louder than it needs to be.
When we avoid something that scares us, we feel better for a moment. But over time the fear usually grows, because we never learn that we can cope.
Being brave does not mean that you have no fear. It means that you feel afraid and do the thing anyway, even if your voice shakes.
Stories about courage often focus on big, dramatic leaps, but most real courage is small and quiet. It happens in kitchens and offices, and it builds up one step at a time.
Here is the central idea of this book, and it is very simple. Do one small brave thing that takes ten minutes or less, and do it often.
Ten minutes is short enough that almost anyone can bear it. If you feel too afraid, you may stop when the timer rings, and that knowledge makes starting much easier.
Priya sits down with a pencil and writes a brave list. It contains small, specific things that frighten her, such as asking a question or speaking to a stranger.
Next, Priya gives each item a number from one to ten to show how scary it feels. Saying hello to the neighbour is a two, and speaking in the meeting is a five.
Priya does not begin with the hardest item, which she rated as a nine. She picks something easy, because early success gives her the confidence to try the harder things.
Priya has lived in her building for a year, and she has never learned her neighbour's name. Her first brave act is to say hello and ask it.
Before she goes out, Priya sets a timer for ten minutes and breathes slowly. She breathes in for four seconds and out for six, and she feels her shoulders drop a little.
Priya knocks, and Mrs Okafor answers with a smile. Priya's heart beats hard for a moment, then it slows, and the two women are soon chatting about the plants on the stairs.
Afterwards, Priya compares what she feared with what really happened. She had imagined a cold stare, but she got a warm smile instead, and she wants to remember that.
Priya makes two columns in her notebook, one for what she feared and one for what happened. Over the weeks, this page becomes a quiet collection of evidence that her fears often exaggerate.
After each brave act, Priya stops and says to herself, That was brave. It feels a little silly at first, but it teaches her mind that effort is worth noticing.
A few weeks later, Priya is ready for her next act, which is a five on her list. She wants to ask one question in the Thursday team meeting.
Priya prepares by writing her question on a sticky note. A short, clear question is easier to say than one that she has to invent in the middle of the room.
Before the meeting, Priya goes into an empty room and reads her question aloud once. Hearing her own voice say it makes the words feel more familiar.
Researchers have found that people tend to think others notice them far more than they really do. In the meeting, most of Priya's colleagues are thinking about their own work.
Priya takes a deep breath, raises her hand and asks her question. For a second there is silence, and then a colleague says that it is a good question.
Priya's voice shakes slightly when she begins to speak in front of everyone. She notices it, takes a breath and carries on, and nobody seems to mind at all.
In the next meeting, Priya makes a small mistake and uses the wrong word. She laughs, corrects herself, and the meeting goes on as before, and the world does not end.
When something goes wrong, we often speak to ourselves more harshly than we would to a friend. Priya tries to ask herself what she would say to a friend in the same situation.
Priya notices a harsh voice in her head that says she will fail. She gives it a funny name, Mr Grumble, and she answers calmly, Thank you, but I am going to try anyway.
On her phone, everyone looks happy and sure of themselves. Priya reminds herself that people show their best moments, and she knows that they also have hard days.
Over coffee, Priya tells her friend Sam about her fears. Sam listens and says that he feels the same way sometimes, and Priya feels much lighter.
At work, Priya cannot work out a difficult spreadsheet. She has been afraid to ask for help because she thinks that she will look stupid.
Priya asks Sam to explain the spreadsheet, and he is glad to help. Most people like to be asked, because helping makes them feel useful and a little closer to the other person.
In a meeting, someone asks a question that Priya cannot answer. She says, I don't know, but I will find out, and she is surprised by how calm she feels afterwards.
Priya has trouble saying no, and she often agrees to extra work that she does not have time for. A polite no, she learns, is not rude but honest, and it protects her time for the things that matter.
To make it easier, Priya writes a short script: “Thank you for asking, but I cannot take that on this week.” She practises it again and again until it feels quite natural to say.
Priya realises that she was short-tempered with a colleague last week, and the thought has been bothering her. A good apology is simple and specific, and she decides to make one.
Priya tells Dan that she is sorry for being short with him, and she does not make excuses. Dan thanks her and says that he had already forgotten about it, and the awkwardness disappears.
For years, Priya has drawn in secret, because she is afraid that others will laugh. Sharing something she cares about is the hardest item on her list, and it is a nine.
Priya joins a weekly drawing class and, after a month, she shows one drawing to the group. She breaks it into steps of ten minutes, and the final step is simply to hold it up.
Not every response to her drawing is warm, and not every voice is kind. A man in the class criticises her drawing unkindly, and Priya feels hurt, but she asks whether any of it is useful.
Priya decides that his remark about proportions is useful, and she keeps it. His tone, however, was careless, and she lets that part go without carrying it around.
Priya auditions for a local choir, and she is not chosen. It hurts, but she knows that she was brave to try, and that failure is a kind of information.
Priya learns that she needs rest as well as courage, so she does not try to do something brave every day. A good rule is to stay just a little outside the comfort zone and not far beyond it.
After some months, Priya looks again at her brave list and sees that the numbers have changed. The neighbour is now a zero, and the question in the meeting is a two.
Priya decides that she is ready for a bigger act. She wants to present her idea to the whole team, and she rates it a seven.
Priya breaks the big presentation into small pieces of ten minutes each. She writes the outline, makes three slides, practises once, and so on, until every piece seems possible.
On the day, Priya's hands shake for the first minute, and her voice sounds thin. Then she finds her place, and her nerves settle as she begins to talk about something that she cares about.
The presentation is not perfect, and she forgets one point. However, her team likes the idea, and her manager asks her to start a small project.
Priya learns to ask which brave acts are really important to her. She does not need to do something scary just to impress other people, but to live in the way that she wants.
A year after the first meeting, Priya still feels afraid at times, and she does not mind. She makes a new brave list for the next year, with new things on it.
Here is the whole idea of the book, in just a few short lines. Do one small brave act that takes ten minutes or less, be kind to yourself, notice what really happens, and keep going.
C1C2: In the Thursday meeting Priya had an idea that she believed in, yet her hand refused to rise and the moment slipped past. As she walked back to her desk afterwards, she felt a familiar mixture of relief and regret, the feeling of having escaped something that she had actually wanted to do. She wondered, as she stared at the screen, whether it might be possible to become braver in small and entirely ordinary ways.

Priya imagined that everybody else walked through life without a flicker of nerves, but she was mistaken. Fear is an ordinary human feeling, shared by the confident and the shy alike, and having it is not a sign that anything is wrong with you. The people who seem confident have usually just learned to act while they are still feeling afraid, which is a skill and not a gift.

When we feel afraid, the body reacts within a moment: the heart speeds up, the palms become damp and the breathing grows shallow. These changes are part of an ancient alarm system that prepares us to fight or to run, and they are not signs of weakness. Knowing that the feeling is physical, and that it passes, can make the whole experience a little less alarming than it first appears.

The alarm system evolved to protect us from physical danger, yet it often rings just as loudly when the only threat is an awkward silence or a room full of faces. It resembles a smoke alarm that goes off whenever someone makes toast, and it is doing its job rather too enthusiastically. We can thank it for the warning and then decide for ourselves whether the danger is real.

When we avoid something that frightens us, we feel an immediate rush of relief, and the mind records that avoiding works. Over time, however, the fear tends to grow, since we never give ourselves the chance to discover that we could have coped. Avoidance feels like safety, but it is more often a slow way of making the world smaller.

Courage is not the absence of fear but the decision to act while it is still present. A brave person feels the same racing heart and the same dry mouth as everyone else, and goes ahead regardless, sometimes with a trembling voice. Every act of courage, however small it may seem to others, is built on this one simple and repeated choice.

Stories about courage tend to feature dramatic leaps, such as the rescue, the speech or the resignation, but most real courage is small and quiet and takes place in ordinary rooms. It accumulates one modest step at a time, just as a muscle grows by lifting small weights often. You do not have to be a hero; you have to be willing to begin.

Here is the central idea of Priya's year: choose one small brave act that takes no more than ten minutes, and then do it, again and again. The act is not meant to be heroic, only a little bit uncomfortable and a little bit beyond what you did yesterday. Fear tends to shrink when you keep meeting it in portions that you can manage, and it grows when you run away from it.

Ten minutes is short enough that almost anyone can bear almost anything for that long. When the timer rings, you are allowed to stop, and the knowledge that there is a way out makes the beginning far less frightening. Very often, however, you will find that you do not wish to stop at all.

Priya sat down with a pencil and wrote what she called her brave list, which was a catalogue of small, specific things that made her uneasy. It included asking a question in a meeting, talking to her neighbour, saying no to a favour and showing her drawings to someone. The more precise each item became, the less shapeless and overwhelming her fear seemed, until it looked like a list of jobs.

Next she gave every item a number from one to ten according to how frightening it felt. Greeting the neighbour was a two, asking a question in the meeting was a five, and showing her drawings to a stranger was a nine that made her stomach turn. Measuring a fear, even roughly, turns it from a vague cloud into a thing that you can plan around and gradually approach.

Priya did not begin with the nine, as that would have been like trying to lift the heaviest weight on the first day at the gym. She picked an easy item, because early success builds confidence, and confidence is what pays for the harder steps. The aim of the first few weeks was simply to prove to herself that she could.

Priya had lived in her building for a year without ever learning her neighbour's name, and the silence in the corridor had become more awkward with every month. Her first brave act was a simple one: to say hello properly and ask it. It was only a two on her list, but her heart still beat as if she were about to cross a high bridge.

Before she opened the door, Priya set a timer for ten minutes and breathed slowly, in for four seconds and out for six, in the way that she had read could calm the body. Her shoulders dropped a little, although her heart still hammered against her ribs like a small and impatient fist. She reminded herself that the feeling did not have to disappear before she was allowed to act.

Priya knocked, and the door was opened by an elderly woman who smiled warmly at the sight of her. For a few seconds Priya's heart pounded, then it eased, as fear generally does when it has been faced, and soon the two women were chatting happily about the plants on the stairs. The neighbour's name, it turned out, was Mrs Okafor, and she had been wondering for a year why the girl next door never spoke.

Afterwards Priya compared what she had feared with what had actually happened, and the gap between them was striking. She had expected a cold stare or an embarrassing silence, and she had received a warm smile and an invitation to tea. The mind, she realised, often paints elaborate pictures of disasters that reality, on the whole, never bothers to produce.

Priya drew two columns in her notebook: one headed what I feared, the other headed what happened. Over the following weeks the page became a quiet collection of evidence, and a pattern emerged in which the fears were nearly always larger than the facts. Writing the comparison down gave her something to read on the days when her courage ran low.

After each brave act, Priya paused and told herself, quite sincerely, that it had been brave. It felt a little silly at first, but the habit taught her mind that effort deserved to be noticed and not only results. Celebrating the small steps is not vanity; it is fuel for the next ones.

A few weeks later Priya felt ready for the next item on her brave list, which was a five: asking one question in the Thursday team meeting. It was a modest goal, but it frightened her far more than the neighbour had done, because it took place in front of her colleagues. She decided to meet it in the same way as before, with a timer, a slow breath and ten calm minutes.

Priya prepared by writing her question on a sticky note, in as few words as she could manage. A short, clear question is far easier to deliver than one that has to be invented in the middle of a room full of people, and the paper acted as a small safety net. Preparation does not remove fear, but it takes away one of its favourite tools, which is surprise.

Before the meeting began, Priya slipped into an empty room and read her question aloud, once, to the chairs. Hearing her own voice say the words made them feel familiar and less dangerous, in the way that a path feels shorter once you have walked it. A single rehearsal, rather than a dozen, was enough to take the edge off her nerves.

Psychologists have found that people tend to overestimate how closely others are watching them, a tendency sometimes called the spotlight effect. Priya looked around the meeting table and saw colleagues glancing at their notes, checking the time and rehearsing their own contributions. They were far too busy with their own worries to analyse her every word.

Priya raised her hand, and her question came out in a voice that was only slightly higher than usual. There was a brief silence, which seemed to last for an hour, and then a colleague nodded and said that it was a good point that nobody had thought of. Priya sat back, surprised that so small an act had cost so much and returned so much more.

Her voice trembled a little as she spoke, and she noticed that the shaking was the loudest thing in the room, at least to her own ears. She took a breath, slowed down, and carried on, and the others waited with plain, ordinary patience. A wobble in the voice is not a failure; it is only the sound of someone doing something that matters to her.

In the following meeting Priya used the wrong word in the middle of a sentence and felt the old heat rise in her cheeks. She laughed, corrected herself and carried on, and the discussion moved ahead as though nothing had happened, which, in truth, nothing had. A small mistake is rarely the catastrophe that the mind announces it to be.

When something goes wrong, we frequently speak to ourselves in a way that we would never use with a friend. Priya began to ask herself what she would say if the same thing had happened to someone she cared about, and the answer was always kinder than her first thought. Self-criticism, it seems, motivates less well than we imagine; gentleness helps us to try again.

Priya noticed a harsh voice in her head that predicted failure at every turn, and she decided to give it a silly name, Mr Grumble. When he started his usual speech, she answered calmly, Thank you for your concern, but I am going to try anyway. Naming the critic did not silence it, but it made the voice sound like one opinion and not like the truth.

On her phone everyone seemed cheerful, confident and effortlessly successful, and Priya felt small beside them. Then she reminded herself that people show their best moments to the world and keep their worries to themselves, so the comparison was not a fair one. Judging your whole life against someone else's highlights is a game that nobody can win.

Over coffee one Saturday, Priya told her friend Sam about her brave list and about how frightened she had been. Sam listened without interrupting and then confessed that he too often felt afraid before speaking in front of people. Priya felt lighter at once, as if a weight that she had been carrying alone had suddenly been shared.

At work Priya was stuck on a complicated spreadsheet, and for two days she struggled with it alone because she feared that asking for help would make her look foolish. Eventually she saw that her silence was costing her more than any question could. Many people hide their difficulties for exactly this reason, and many of them suffer for it unnecessarily.

Priya summoned her courage and asked Sam to explain the spreadsheet, and he agreed at once with obvious pleasure. Most people are glad to be asked for help, since being useful to another person feels good and tends to make the two of them feel closer. Her fear had been the larger of the two problems, and it was solved in twenty minutes.

In a meeting a colleague asked Priya a question to which she did not know the answer, and her first instinct was to bluff. Instead she said plainly that she did not know but would find out, and she was surprised by how calm she felt, and how much respect the honesty seemed to earn. Pretending to know everything is exhausting, and admitting that you do not is a relief.

Priya had always found it hard to say no, and she often agreed to extra tasks that she had no time to finish, and then resented them. She learned that a polite no is not rudeness but honesty, and that it protects your time and your energy for the things that matter most. It also makes your yes worth a great deal more, since people can trust that it was freely given.

To make the task easier, Priya wrote a short script that she could use when the moment came: thank you for asking, but I cannot take that on this week. She practised it in the mirror until the words came easily, because a sentence you have prepared is far simpler to say under pressure than one you must invent. A brave act, in the end, is very often nothing more than a practised one, repeated until it feels ordinary.

Priya realised that she had been short-tempered with a colleague called Dan the week before, and the memory had been nagging at her ever since. A good apology is simple, specific and free of excuses, and it takes a certain amount of courage because it admits that we were wrong. She decided that it was an eight on her list, and that it was time.

Priya found Dan at the coffee machine and told him that she was sorry for being sharp with him, without adding an excuse or a justification. Dan thanked her warmly and said that he had already half forgotten the incident, and the knot in her stomach dissolved at once. A sincere apology, she saw, repairs far more than it costs, and it restores a kind of ease between two people.

For years Priya had drawn in secret, filling notebooks with trees, hands and faces that nobody else ever saw. The fear of being laughed at kept them hidden, because to share something that you care about is to risk being hurt by the response. This was the nine on her brave list, and she had been circling it for months.

Priya joined a weekly drawing class and, after a month, plucked up the courage to show a single drawing to the group. She broke the task into ten-minute steps: choosing the drawing, framing it, travelling there and finally holding it up for others to see. The reception was warm, and one classmate asked whether she could teach her how to draw hands.

Not every response to her work was warm, and the world is never made up only of kind people. A man in the class made an unkind remark about her drawing, and the sting was real, but after a moment Priya asked herself whether there was anything useful in what he had said. Criticism that is specific and offered with respect deserves attention, whereas mere scorn can be set aside without a moment's guilt.

Priya concluded that one part of his remark, about the proportions of the face, was genuinely useful, and she kept it. His careless tone, however, said more about him than about her work, and she allowed it to float away. Learning to sort feedback in this way, accepting the lesson and refusing the insult, is a skill that protects both your courage and your improvement.

Priya, feeling bold, auditioned for a local choir, and a week later she received a polite email saying that she had not been chosen. It hurt, naturally, but she reminded herself that the courage lay in trying and not in winning, and that every failure carries information about what to practise next. She wrote down two things that she had learned from the experience, and then she went home to practise them.

Priya learned that courage needs rest as well as effort, so she stopped trying to do something frightening every single day. A good guide is to stay just outside the comfort zone and not far beyond it, because a fear that overwhelms you teaches you nothing. If fear stops you from living normally, a doctor or a therapist can help, and this book is general information and not a treatment.

After a few months Priya looked again at her brave list and saw that the numbers had changed. The neighbour had fallen to a zero, the question in the meeting to a two, and even sharing a drawing had dropped from a nine to a six. Psychologists have long found that facing fears gradually, in small steps, tends to make them shrink, and Priya was living proof.

Priya decided that she was ready for a larger challenge, and she chose to present her idea to the entire team, which she rated as a seven. The idea that had slipped away in January was still waiting for her, and it had grown better with time. She meant to deliver it, not perfectly, but with her whole attention and with every ounce of honesty that she could muster.

Priya broke the great task into small parts that each took ten minutes: sketching the outline, writing the opening, making three slides, practising the first minute and practising the last. Each piece was manageable in itself, and none of them felt like a leap. A big brave act, she discovered, is usually a staircase wearing the disguise of a cliff.

On the day of the presentation Priya's hands trembled for the first minute, and her voice sounded thin and unfamiliar in the large room. Then she found her place, and as she began to speak about something that she truly cared about, her nerves slowly settled. Fear, she noticed, tends to peak at the beginning and then loosen its grip as the action takes over.

The presentation was far from perfect, for she forgot one of her points and ran a little over time. Nevertheless the team liked the idea, and her manager asked her to lead a small trial of it. What she remembered afterwards was less the mistakes than the simple feeling of having stood up and said what she thought.

Priya learned to ask which brave acts really mattered to her, instead of doing frightening things merely to impress others. Courage in the service of your own values, such as honesty, creativity or kindness, is far more satisfying than courage for show. She began to choose her ten-minute challenges according to the person she wanted to become.

A year after that silent Thursday meeting, Priya still felt afraid from time to time, and she no longer expected otherwise. What had changed was her relationship to the fear, which she now regarded as a companion who sometimes got too loud, not as a judge. She turned to a fresh page and began a new brave list, with entirely new items on it.

Here, then, is the whole idea of the book, gathered together into a few lines that you can carry in your pocket. Choose one small act that frightens you a little, give it ten minutes, and be as kind to yourself as you would be to a friend. Do it again tomorrow and the day after, because courage is not a gift that some people are born with but a muscle that grows with every small act of use.
